capabilities.label: Primitive
capabilities.means: Key generation, encapsulation or signing, and the matching decapsulation or verification, through the component's own API.
capabilities.default_means: Registered and selectable through the default provider or backend with no build flag or opt-in.

capabilities.label: TLS 1.3
capabilities.means: Use in a TLS 1.3 handshake -- key exchange for a KEM or hybrid group, authentication for a signature scheme.
capabilities.default_means: In the default supported-groups list (key exchange) or the default signature-algorithms list (authentication) as shipped.

capabilities.label: X.509
capabilities.means: Certificates and keys -- generating, parsing, signing, verifying and chain-building with the algorithm; composite and hybrid forms where the algorithm is one.
capabilities.default_means: Accepted in chain verification without an opt-in.

capabilities.label: SSH
capabilities.means: Use in the SSH key exchange or as a host or user key type.
capabilities.default_means: In the default key-exchange or key-type preference list as shipped.

capabilities.label: IPsec / IKEv2
capabilities.means: Use in IKEv2 key exchange or authentication.
capabilities.default_means: In the default IKEv2 proposal as shipped.

capabilities.label: FIPS 140-3
capabilities.means: Standing of the algorithm inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module of the component. See the file header for how the scale reads here.
capabilities.default_means: Inside the validated boundary and enabled in the module's approved mode.

algorithms.label: X25519MLKEM768
algorithms.note: The hybrid group browsers and CDNs deploy. Pre-standard name X25519Kyber768.

algorithms.label: curveSM2MLKEM768
algorithms.note: Added so a component that ships it (OpenSSL 4.0) can be recorded; expect few cells.

algorithms.label: ML-DSA
algorithms.note: External-mu (pre-hashed mu) signing is recorded in the cell note, not as a row, until two components track it.

algorithms.label: FN-DSA (Falcon)
algorithms.note: Pre-standard Falcon-512/1024 support is recorded here with the note saying so.

algorithms.label: Composite ML-DSA
algorithms.note: ML-DSA paired with an ECDSA, EdDSA or RSA component in one X.509 signature.

why.composite: The composite drafts register X.509 and CMS algorithm identifiers. TLS has no SignatureScheme codepoint for a composite, so nothing can offer one in a handshake; a composite certificate inside a verified chain is the x509 cell, not this one.
why.stateful-hbs: TLS registers no SignatureScheme for LMS or XMSS, and an online handshake signer -- one key, many signatures, no shared state -- is precisely the use SP 800-208 excludes.

why.hybrid-kex: These rows are named TLS groups: an IANA TLS codepoint negotiated in a handshake, never a certificate key type. A certificate holding an ML-KEM key is the kem row.
SSH names its own hybrid key exchanges (mlkem768x25519-sha256 and kin) rather than borrowing the TLS groups these rows hold, so an SSH hybrid is recorded against the KEM row it is built from.
why.composite: SSH defines no key type or key-exchange method using a composite signature; the composite work is X.509 and CMS.
why.stateful-hbs: SSH registers no LMS or XMSS key type, and a host key signs on every connection, which a stateful signer cannot safely do.

why.hybrid-kex: RFC 9370 composes additional key exchanges from single transforms rather than negotiating a TLS group, so an IKEv2 hybrid is recorded against the KEM row it is built from.
why.composite: No IKEv2 implementation or draft defines a composite signature for RFC 7427 authentication. The ASN.1 encoding could in principle carry one, so flip this the day a draft says so.
why.stateful-hbs: IKEv2 registers no LMS or XMSS authentication method.

why.composite: No composite scheme appears in a FIPS standard. CMVP validates the ML-DSA and the ECDSA or RSA component separately, which the signature rows already carry.

except.why: FIPS 206 is still a draft, so there is no standard to validate against and CMVP will not certify a pre-standard scheme. A real question again on the day FIPS 206 is final.
SM2 is not a NIST-approved curve, so the group cannot sit inside a FIPS 140-3 approved boundary whatever the ML-KEM half does.

categories.label: Libraries and Language Stacks
categories.blurb: The code almost everything else inherits its cryptography from: the general-purpose libraries, the language standard libraries and runtimes, and the protocol implementations that sit directly on them. This is where a migration usually starts, because a component here decides what thousands of applications can negotiate.

categories.label: Hardware and Key Management
categories.blurb: Where keys are generated and held rather than used: hardware security modules and the cloud key management services built on them. Readiness here gates what a regulated deployment may do at all, and it moves on validation timelines rather than release timelines.

categories.label: Platforms and Edge
categories.blurb: The systems and intermediaries between an application and the wire: operating system cryptographic stacks, the proxies and load balancers that terminate TLS, and the tooling that issues certificates. A component here can enable post-quantum protection for software that knows nothing about it.

questions.title: Which components can sign with pure ML-DSA today?
questions.blurb: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) through the component's own API, in a general release, without a build flag or preview channel. Pure rather than composite: this asks about ML-DSA on its own, not paired with a classical algorithm in one signature. The bar is `available`, so a component that ships it but does not select it by default still counts -- the question is whether you can use it, not whether you get it without asking.

questions.title: Which components can negotiate a hybrid post-quantum TLS group?
questions.blurb: Any one of the IANA-registered hybrid key exchange groups -- X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 -- usable in a TLS 1.3 handshake in a general release. Hybrid rather than pure ML-KEM because hybrid is what browsers and CDNs actually deploy: the classical half means a flaw in the lattice half is not fatal. The bar is `available`, so a group you must configure counts here; the stricter question is the next one.

questions.title: Which components offer a hybrid post-quantum TLS group with no configuration?
questions.blurb: The same three groups as the previous question, but at the bar that matters for traffic actually on the wire: `default`, meaning the group is in the supported-groups list as shipped. This is the question behind "is my fleet already protected against harvest now, decrypt later?", because a group nobody enables protects nobody.

questions.title: Which components can handle ML-DSA X.509 certificates?
questions.blurb: ML-DSA in certificates and keys -- generating, parsing, signing, verifying or chain-building -- in a general release. The bar is `available`. This is the question that decides whether a post-quantum PKI is deployable at all, and it is deliberately separate from the TLS questions: a stack can negotiate a hybrid key exchange while being unable to validate a post-quantum certificate, and most can.

questions.title: Which components have ML-KEM inside a FIPS 140-3 validated module?
questions.blurb: ML-KEM named in the approved-algorithm list of a module with an ISSUED CMVP certificate -- not a FIPS build, not a submission in the queue, not a vendor's announcement. The bar is `available`, which on the FIPS scale means inside the validated boundary. Running in an approved mode additionally needs the validated version on a tested operating environment, which no register can tell you; this question answers only whether the algorithm is inside the boundary at all.

components.name: Apple CryptoKit and corecrypto
components.release_channel: Annual operating system releases. Post-quantum support arrived across the board in the 26 releases.

cells.since: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS 26, tvOS 26 and watchOS 26

evidence.note: Apple Platform Security: post-quantum support "was added in the Apple CryptoKit framework in iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS 26, tvOS 26, and watchOS 26", naming ML-KEM 768 and ML-KEM 1024.

cells.note: Two parameter sets only -- ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. ML-KEM-512 is not named, which for a platform that ships one curated API surface is worth reading as a deliberate omission rather than an oversight, though the page does not say so.

cells.since: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS 26, tvOS 26 and watchOS 26

evidence.note: Same page, for authentication: ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87.

cells.note: ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 only; ML-DSA-44 is not named. The same curation as the KEM parameter sets.

gaps.why: The same shape as Windows, from the same scan. Apple holds 32 corecrypto certificates and the one read in detail (5387, Apple corecrypto Module 18.3 [Apple silicon, Kernel, Software, SL1]) lists 52 approved algorithms, none post-quantum. Two Apple corecrypto Module OS 26 submissions have been in Review since 30 and 31 July 2026, and OS 26 is exactly the release that shipped ML-KEM to CryptoKit -- so the pending modules are the ones that would carry it, and calling this absent would be wrong. Second pass: those certificates when they issue.
sources: CMVP validated module search, vendor Apple (32 corecrypto modules)

gaps.why: As ML-KEM, and for the same reason: shipped in CryptoKit with the 26 releases, absent from every issued corecrypto certificate, and blocked from absence by the OS 26 modules still in Review.

The Apple Platform Security page names ML-KEM and ML-DSA and no other post-quantum family. It is an overview rather than an API enumeration, so this is unknown, NOT a cited absence -- the distinction the register exists to keep. Second pass: the CryptoKit framework reference on developer.apple.com, which does enumerate types.
sources: Apple Platform Security, Quantum-secure cryptography in Apple operating systems

gaps.why: As SLH-DSA: not named on the page read, and the page does not enumerate. Apple signs firmware, so stateful hash-based signatures are a question worth asking of corecrypto specifically.
sources: Apple Platform Security, Quantum-secure cryptography in Apple operating systems

components.name: Apple Network framework and URLSession
components.release_channel: Annual operating system releases, with the rest of the platform.

cells.since: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS 26, tvOS 26 and watchOS 26

evidence.note: "Apple supports quantum-secure encryption in TLS in the developer networking APIs URLSession and Network frameworks", and these "enable it by default for all systems services and apps that use them."

cells.note: `default` is the whole point of this cell and is unusual in this register: an application that does nothing at all gets post-quantum key exchange, because the frameworks turn it on for everything built against them. That is a stronger claim than any library's default-group list, since it reaches software whose authors never considered the question.

gaps.why: Apple states that quantum-secure TLS is on by default but does not name the negotiated group, and this register records hybrid groups one row per NAMED group. Recording X25519MLKEM768 on the strength of it being the group everyone else deploys would be exactly the plausible-looking guess the register refuses. Second pass: Apple developer documentation or a WWDC session naming the group, or a packet capture, which is evidence of a different kind.
sources: Apple Platform Security, Quantum-secure cryptography in Apple operating systems

derives_from.why: The networking frameworks do no cryptography of their own; corecrypto does, and corecrypto is what Apple submits for validation. The FIPS answer here is therefore CryptoKit and corecrypto's.

components.name: aws-lc-rs
components.release_channel: Rust crate over AWS-LC; numbered releases.

cells.note: Stable API without the unstable feature flag from 1.18.1; described as not fully stabilised in February 2026.

evidence.note: Security policy for certificate 5314, AWS-LC 3 Cryptographic Module (static), module version AWS-LC FIPS 3.1.0. The string ML-DSA does not occur in it; ML-KEM occurs 101 times.
AWS's own certificate list: AWS-LC-FIPS v3.1 is certificates 5298 (dynamic) and 5314 (static). No v3.0 certificate is listed.

cells.note: RESOLVED 2026-09-13, downgraded from `available` after the verification the earlier flag asked for. The chain, end to end: aws-lc-rs's FIPS build pulls aws-lc-fips-sys, whose own README says it binds AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x (branch fips-2024-09-27); AWS's FIPS.md attributes certificates 5298 (dynamic) and 5314 (static) to that module line; and the security policy for 5314 -- read in full -- does not contain the string ML-DSA anywhere, not even among the non-approved algorithms, while ML-KEM appears 101 times. So ML-DSA is in the FIPS-branch library the crate builds and is NOT in the validated boundary of any AWS-LC module NIST has certified, which is exactly what this scale calls `experimental`: in a module build that is not the validated one. The crate's own release note ("including under FIPS") is about the FIPS BUILD, and that was the ambiguity: a FIPS build is not a FIPS validation. One thread is deliberately left hanging rather than papered over -- see the ml-kem/fips gap: the crate documents binding 3.0.x while the certified module is 3.1.0, and no public document read on 2026-09-13 closes that minor-version gap. It does not affect THIS cell, because ML-DSA is absent under either version.

cells.since: documented at 1.18.1; first release not stated
cells.note: The kem module documents ML_KEM_512, ML_KEM_768 and ML_KEM_1024 as a stable public API, not behind the unstable feature flag that gated ML-DSA until 1.18.1. The docs name no introducing version.

gaps.why: Not an absence -- an unclosed link, recorded so the next pass does not redo the reading. ML-KEM IS inside the validated boundary: the security policy for certificate 5314 (AWS-LC FIPS 3.1.0) names ML-KEM 101 times, and the certificate's approved-algorithm list carries ML-KEM KeyGen and EncapDecap. What is not established is that the module this CRATE carries is that module: aws-lc-fips-sys documents binding AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x, AWS's FIPS.md lists certificates for v1.0, v2.0, v3.1 and NetOS but none for v3.0, and the crate page for the published 0.14.2 repeats the same 3.0.x wording. Writing `available` would assert a minor-version match that no document read makes. What would settle it: a statement from AWS-LC-FIPS or the crate naming the module version the released crate bundles, or a build that reports it.
sources: aws-lc-fips-sys README (main branch and the published 0.14.2 crate page)

derives_from.pinned: AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x per aws-lc-fips-sys; the certified module on that line is 3.1.0
derives_from.why: The crate is a Rust binding over AWS-LC: docs.rs lists aws-lc-sys for the ordinary build and aws-lc-fips-sys for the FIPS one among its dependencies. The FIPS module that binding carries was traced on 2026-09-13 -- AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x by the crate's own README -- which settled the ml-dsa/fips cell (ML-DSA is in no AWS-LC certificate at all) and left one minor-version question open, recorded as the ml-kem/fips gap. The `pinned` value states both halves rather than choosing one.

evidence.note: Dependencies listed for 1.18.1: aws-lc-fips-sys ^0.14.2 and aws-lc-sys ^0.45.0, both optional.
"Currently, aws-lc-fips-sys binds to AWS-LC-FIPS 3.0.x" (branch fips-2024-09-27), and the crate binds the latest module SUBMITTED to NIST, which is not the same as the latest certified.

components.name: BoringSSL
components.release_channel: Rolling, no numbered releases; consumers pin commits (Chrome, Android, Envoy).

cells.note: Chrome shipped it by default from 131 with the standard codepoint; whether BoringSSL's own default group list carries it is a conflict in the ledger (d0001:23).
One source dates ML-DSA to April 2026 instead (ledger conflict d0005:1).
ML-DSA-87 certificate validation plus OIDs/NIDs for ML-DSA and ML-KEM.
A pure ML-KEM group is supported: kNamedGroups carries MLKEM1024 (SSL_GROUP_MLKEM1024) alongside the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid. MLKEM768 and MLKEM512 are not in the array.

Asymmetric, and the asymmetry matters: ML-DSA-44/65/87 sit at positions 1 to 3 of kSignSignatureAlgorithms, the default list for SIGNING, but appear nowhere in kVerifySignatureAlgorithms, the default list for VERIFYING. BoringSSL will therefore offer an ML-DSA signature by default and still not accept one by default, so this is 'available', not 'default'.

Absent from kNamedGroups, which is the exhaustive list of groups libssl knows. Recorded as 'none' rather than a gap because an exhaustive array makes the absence a positive finding, not an open question.
Absent from kNamedGroups, as above.

evidence.note: Three Google BoringCrypto modules were in the CMVP queue on this date, at Comment Resolution - Lab since 6 May, 5 June and 6 July 2026.

cells.note: A queue position, not a shipped capability. CORRECTED by the 2026-09-12 CMVP reverse scan: Google DOES validate BoringCrypto and holds seven certificates for it (5296, 5244, 5104, 4735, 4444, 4407, 4156), so the earlier reading that BoringSSL had never pursued validation was wrong. derives_from.why: On Linux .NET's cryptography is the operating system's. Microsoft's own cross-platform cryptography document states that .NET apps have access to FIPS-validated algorithms if the OS libraries are FIPS-validated, and that Linux requires OpenSSL 3. This entry is the LINUX half; the Windows half is the CNG edge below, and macOS is neither -- the same document records that OpenSSL support on macOS was removed, and .NET's post-quantum APIs need CNG or an OpenSSL that has the algorithms, so macOS has no recorded post-quantum path at all.

derives_from.why: The Windows half of the same document: .NET's cryptography on Windows is CNG's, and its post-quantum APIs require a Windows whose CNG has the algorithms. PROMOTED from an `external` edge the same day the platform pass made Windows CNG a component -- which is what the promotion invariant in the validator exists to force, and it did: the check fired on this edge before anyone remembered it was here.

evidence.note: "Windows Cryptography API Next Generation (CNG) is used whenever new RSACng() is used"; and .NET apps have access to FIPS-validated algorithms if the OS libraries are FIPS-validated.

components.name: Java (OpenJDK)
components.release_channel: Two feature releases a year; LTS every two years with backports via quarterly CPUs.

cells.note: JEP 496: native JCA engine classes, ML-KEM-512/768/1024.
JEP 497; JAR signing with ML-DSA from JDK 26.
keytool generates ML-KEM key pairs and certificates; the certificate must be signed with a signature algorithm.

JEP 527 delivers hybrid TLS 1.3 key exchange in JDK 27, and the Curve25519 optimisation claim names X25519MLKEM768 as a group whose key generation it speeds up. Neither claim states the default group list, so 'available', not 'default'.

JEP 497, delivered in JDK 24: keytool generates ML-DSA key pairs and certificates, and KeyFactory converts an ML-DSA public key to and from its X.509 encoding. components.name: RHEL system-wide crypto-policies
components.release_channel: RHEL minor releases. The post-quantum position changed materially between 10.0 and 10.1, which is what the cells below record.

evidence.note: "post-quantum cryptography with Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) and ML-DSA in TLS is generally available and fully supported in Go, OpenSSL, GnuTLS and NSS", and from 10.1 "applications that use OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, or the Go programming language have support for post-quantum key exchange enabled by default".

The 10.0 position, for contrast: ML-KEM is available for TLS in OpenSSL, GnuTLS and NSS, but the system-wide policy must be switched -- "dnf install crypto-policies-pq-preview crypto-policies-scripts" then "update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:TEST-PQ", with the note that the package and policy name are subject to change.

cells.note: The version boundary is the finding, and it is why this component exists as its own row rather than as a note on OpenSSL. On RHEL 10.0 post-quantum key exchange is EXPERIMENTAL in this register's sense -- gated behind a preview package and a named policy module. On 10.1 the same libraries, unchanged, are default because the policy changed. RHEL 9.7 sits in between: the blog records that OpenSSL- and NSS-based applications there can use post-quantum TLS by enabling the policy module with "update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:PQ". A NO-PQ subpolicy turns it back off, so this is a default somebody can revoke centrally -- which is the whole purpose of the layer.

evidence.note: The worked example shows the negotiated group by name in an openssl s_client transcript: "Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768".
The 10.1 default that makes it reachable without configuration.

cells.note: Named, so it is recorded on the named-group row rather than left on the KEM family. This is the cell Apple's networking component could not have, for the exact reason recorded in its gap: Red Hat prints the group, Apple does not.

cells.note: Available, not default, and Red Hat says why in the same breath: "no public Certificate Authorities (CAs) currently offer post-quantum cryptography, but private CAs or self-signed certificates can be created with ML-DSA today". A policy can permit an algorithm that nothing in the public web actually presents.

cells.note: Roadmapped, not shipped, and deliberately recorded on the KEM row rather than on a named hybrid group: Microsoft names no group, and inventing one would put a claim in the register that its source does not make. The same announcement shipped ML-KEM and ML-DSA in CNG on the same day, so the gap between the two is the finding -- the primitives are generally available on Windows while the TLS stack that would use them is still a roadmap item.

gaps.why: Which group Schannel will offer is unstated. The announcement says only that TLS support is proceeding in alignment with IETF standards. Second pass: Windows Insider release notes or the Schannel documentation naming a supported group.

derives_from.why: Schannel performs no cryptography of its own; it calls CNG, which is where Windows' validated modules live. Its FIPS standing is therefore CNG's, and the pointer says so rather than repeating it.

evidence.note: Schannel is documented as a security support provider implementing TLS/SSL over the Windows cryptographic providers.

components.name: wolfSSL / wolfCrypt
components.release_channel: Numbered releases (5.9.x); a separate FIPS 140-3 module line.

cells.note: Native implementation; the liboqs dependency was removed by August 2026.
Renamed from Dilithium in 5.9.2.
Sign/verify APIs take pre-hashed digests from 5.9.2.
RFC 9802 LMS/XMSS in X.509 certificate and CSR generation.
TLS 1.3 hybrid and pure groups (multiple SecP*MLKEM* and X*MLKEM*), shown through curl built with wolfSSL.
CertificateVerify and peer certificate verification in TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3.
CAVP algorithm certificate A8437 covers ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS; the module validation itself is announced, not shown as issued.
Peer certificate verification with SLH-DSA, from the same end-to-end support claim as the TLS cell.

wolfSSL names its hybrid groups in its own convention -- WOLFSSL_X25519_ML_KEM_768 is the group the IETF calls X25519MLKEM768 -- and ships an unusually wide set beside it: P256, P384, P521 and X448 pairings across ML-KEM 512, 768 and 1024. The project notes the IETF name does not follow the hybrid draft's own convention, for historical reasons.

rejected.why: About the SEALSQ QVault TPM that wolfTPM now drives, not about wolfCrypt's own standing, which already records ML-KEM and ML-DSA as available. It belongs to a future hsm-kind component (SEALSQ QVault TPM); phase 3's scope decision defers those. Reviewed 2026-09-12.
